'''''Aphanes australis''''' (syn. ''Alchemilla australis''), '''slender parsley-piert''', is a sprawling, downy plant that is found in  acid grassland and on bare ground throughout western Europe and which has spread to other parts of the world with agriculture.

==Description==
Slender parsley-piert is a pale green winter [[Annual plant| annual]] [[herbaceous plant| herb]] with prostrate, branched, leafy  stems up to 15 cm long. The leaves are alternate and spiral around the stem, with a short petiole and large, deeply-lobed [[stipule]]s at the base. They are about 0.5 cm long, broadly ternate with deeply lobed leaflets, and sparsely hairy. An important identification feature is the leaf base, which is usually [[wiktionary:cuneate|cuneate]], narrowing gradually into the stalk.
<ref name="Stace">{{Cite book |last=Stace |first=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |publisher=C&M Floristics |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2 |location=Suffolk}}</ref><ref name=Sell2>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 2 |date=2014 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |ISBN=978-0-521-55336-0}}</ref><ref name=Poland>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref>

The inflorescences are [[wiktionary:glomerule|glomerules]] of 4-10 flowers nestled within the stipules, opposite the base of each leaf. The flowers are up to 2 mm long, pale green, sparsely [[wiktionary:pubescent|pubescent]] and have 4 sepals which never open fully. Petals are absent. Flowers are bisexual, usually with a single stamen and a single style which are almost entirely hidden by the sepals.

Each flower produces a single achene that is ovoid, glabrous and shining.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Aphanes australis : Slender Parsley-piert {{!}} NBN Atlas |url=https://species.nbnatlas.org/species/NBNSYS0100001604#overview |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=species.nbnatlas.org}}</ref>

[[File:Aphanes_australis_sl165.jpg|thumb|The flowers have erect sepals and the leaf base narrows gradually into the stalk.]]

==Identification==
Slender parsley-piert can be very difficult to tell apart from common parsley-piert, although the former tends to be smaller, a brighter green, have cuneate rather than cordate leaf bases, and grows in acid grassland rather than arable fields and waste ground. Those useful field characters can be confirmed by the following observations:
* Slender parsley-piert has flowers that are 1-1.9 mm long, while those of common parsley-piert are 1.9-2.7 mm
* Slender has upright sepals, while common has them spreading
* Slender has smooth fruits, while common has them furrowed at the base
* Slender has deeply divided stipule teeth, while common has them divided less than half way
* Slender has 6-9 leaf lobes, while common has 7-15.<ref name=Bomble>{{Cite journal |last=Bomble |first=F.W. |date=2016 |title=Alchemilla arvensis (Gewöhnlicher Acker-Frauenmantel) und Alchemilla australis (Südlicher Acker-Frauenmantel) in Nordrhein-Westfalen |url=https://www.botanik-bochum.de/jahrbuch/Pflanzenportraet_Alchemilla_Aphanes.pdf |journal=Jahrb. Bochumer Bot. Ver. |volume=7 |pages=159-166}}</ref>
[[File:Aphanes arvensis sl32.jpg|thumb|The flowers of [[Alchemilla arvensis|common parsley-piert]] have spreading sepals, unlike those of slender parsley-piert.]]

==Taxonomy==
The different species of parsley-piert have not always been adequately recognised. [[Carl Linnaeus]], in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' (1753) gave only one species, which he called ''Aphanes arvensis''.<ref name=Linnaeus>{{Cite book |last=Linné |first=Carl von |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/84235#page/139/mode/1up |title=Species plantarum : exhibentes plantas rite cognitas ad genera relatas, cum diferentiis specificis, nominibus trivialibus, synonymis selectis, locis natalibus, secundum systema sexuale digestas |last2=Linné |first2=Carl von |date=1753 |publisher=Junk |volume=t.1 (1753) |location=Berlin}}</ref>
This name would have been used for both ''[[Alchemilla arvensis|Aphanes arvensis]]'' and ''A. australis'' until the latter was recognised as distinct. That happened in 1908, when a review of four North American species of parsley-piert was undertaken by [[Per Axel Rydberg]] of the New York Botanic Garden. He described it from a specimen that had been collected in Washington, D.C., and said it could be found from Virginia to Georgia.<ref>{{Cite book |last=New York Botanical Garden |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15437#page/90/mode/1up |title=North American flora |last2=Garden |first2=New York Botanical |date=1908 |publisher=New York Botanical Garden |volume=v. 22, pt. 4 (1908) |location=[New York]}}</ref> Meanwhile, it had also been described from Spain as early as 1842 and named ''Alchemilla microcarpa'', but was overlooked elsewhere in Europe until the mid-20th century.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Walters |first=S.M. |date=1949 |title=Aphanes microcarpa (Boiss. et Reut.) Rothm. in Britain |url=https://archive.org/details/wats-1p-163 |journal=Watsonia |volume=1 |pages=163-169}}</ref>

The close relationship between ''Aphanes'' and ''Alchemilla'' has long been known. Parsley-piert was even called ''Alchemilla montana minima'' before Linnaeus's time.<ref name="Linnaeus" /> Recent studies have shown that the genus ''Alchemilla'' is [[Polyphyly|polyphyletic]], so either ''Aphanes'' has to be included within that genus, or several new genera need to be named. At present, botanical authors differ in which approach they take.<ref name="Bomble" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Morales-Briones |first=Diego F |last2=Gehrke |first2=Berit |last3=Huang |first3=Chien-Hsun |last4=Liston |first4=Aaron |last5=Ma |first5=Hong |last6=Marx |first6=Hannah E |last7=Tank |first7=David C |last8=Yang |first8=Ya |date=2022-01-01 |title=Analysis of Paralogs in Target Enrichment Data Pinpoints Multiple Ancient Polyploidy Events in Alchemilla s.l. (Rosaceae) |url=https://academic.oup.com/sysbio/article/71/1/190/6274658 |journal=Systematic Biology |volume=71 |issue=1 |pages=190–207 |doi=10.1093/sysbio/syab032 |issn=1063-5157|pmc=8677558 }}</ref> The differences between the parsley-pierts and the lady's-mantles are that the former are annuals while the latter are perennials, and the flowers have a different arrangement of stamens.

The origin of the common name parsley-piert is unknown, but several suggestions have been made. One is that it is derived from [[parsley]], owing to the similarity in shape of the leaves, and a corruption of "pierce", because it was formerly used to treat (or pierce) kidney stones.<ref name=Grieve>{{cite book |last1=Grieve |first1=Maud |title=A Modern Herbal |date=1931 |publisher=Dover Publications Inc. |location=New York |isbn=0-486-22798-7}}</ref> Another is that it comes from the French ''perce-pierre'', meaning "stone-piercer" because of its habit of growing in shallow, stony soil.<ref name=Mabey>{{cite book |last1=Mabey |first1=Richard |title=Flora Britannica |date=1996 |publisher=Reed International |location=London |isbn=1-85619-377-2}}</ref>

==Distribution and status==
Slender parsley-piert occurs throughout Western Europe, excluding the Mediterranean islands and the former [[Czechoslovakia]], as far east as Turkey and southwards to North Africa. Although its scientific name originates from an American study, it is now considered to be an introduction there, where it is found in the eastern states from New York to Texas and on the west coast from Vancouver Island to Oregon. It is also known as an introduction in Australia and New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alchemilla australis (Rydb.) Bomble {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:60476156-2 |access-date=2025-03-23 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Aphanes australis Rydb. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/5365026 |access-date=2025-03-23 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref>

It has not yet been assessed for a global threat status,<ref>{{Cite web |title=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250323065505/https://www.iucnredlist.org/ |archive-date=2025-03-23 |access-date=2025-03-23 |website=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species}}</ref> but in Britain and France it is classes as LC ([[Least-concern species|Least Concern]]), meaning that there is no evidence of a decline.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cheffings |first1=C.M. | last2=Farrell |first2=L. |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain |date=2005 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Museum national d'Histoire naturelle |title=Aphanes australis Rydb., 1908 - Aphane australe, Alchémille oubliée, Alchémille à petits fruits, Alchémille australe |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/83160 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221129073228/https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/83160 |archive-date=2022-11-29 |access-date=2025-03-23 |website=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel |language=fr-FR}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
The [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] of slender parsley-piert in Britain are L=7, F=4, R=5, N=4, S=0, which means it favours moderate light, low moisture, slightly acidic conditions, low nutrients and is salt intolerant.<ref name="Plantatt">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=M.O. |last2=Preston |first2=C.D. |last3=Roy |first3=D.B. |title=PLANTATT - Attributes of British and Irish Plants - Spreadsheet |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/biblio/plantatt-attributes-british-and-irish-plants-spreadsheet |publisher=UK Biological Records Centre}}</ref>

The main habitat for this species in Britain is probably [[Calcifugous grasslands and montane communities in the British National Vegetation Classification system|U1 ''Festuca ovina'' community]], which is an upland acid grassland, typically found on nutrient-poor, acidic soils. It is, however, also recorded on patches of bare soil and sparse vegetation in a variety of habitats, including CG2 ''[[Avenula pratensis]]'', CG3 ''[[Bromus erectus]]'' and CG7 ''[[Festuca ovina]]'' grassland and OV22 ''[[Poa annua]]'' open vegetation community.<ref name=Lockton>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/389889868|isbn=978-0-9530937-2-4}}</ref><ref name=Rodwell>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vols. 1-5 |date=1991–2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref>

The downy mildew ''[[Peronospora|Peronospora oblatispora]]'' is the only disease known to infest this particular species.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Aphanes – Plant Parasites of Europe |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/host-plants/plantae/spermatopsida/angiosperma/eudicots/superrosids/rosids/fabids/rosales/rosaceae/rosoideae/potentilleae/aphanes/ |access-date=2025-03-24 |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref>

==Uses==
There are no recorded uses for slender parsley-piert, but presumably anything that [[Alchemilla arvensis|common parsley-piert]] is used for would also apply to this species.
